Scatter: pixels vs model, over the whole corpus

Every scatter panel the corpus contains, read twice — by the pixel engine and by claude-opus-5 at high effort — and judged on two measures chosen not to presuppose that denser is better.

What is measured, and what was wrong before

The first comparison scored readers on points landing on ink and reported point count as though more were better. Both were biased. Points-on-ink flatters the pixel engine, whose points are derived from ink and sit on it almost by construction, while the model's are produced independently. And a scatter's data is the symbols the authors plotted: cutting a fused run into one point per column oversamples it — 9× the symbol count here, against the model's 0.5×. Neither matches; they miss in opposite directions.

accuracy — distance from each model point to the nearest real data point. trend — take the model's sparse points, join them up, and measure the dense trace against that curve. The second is the question a sparse reading has to answer: if a handful of points reproduces the curve, the handful is enough. Both are computed per matched series and in fractions of the plot box, because the engine emits a 0–1 fraction wherever an axis was never calibrated — 28 of these 53 panels.

Result

measuremedian75th pct90th pct within 1%within 3%within 5%
accuracy1.53%7.65% 39.64%22/53 34/5336/53
trend4.52%15.85% 247.46%7/50 21/5026/50

On the typical panel the sparse reading is good: the model's points sit 1.5% of the plot box from real data, and joining them up reproduces the curve to within 4.5%. That is enough for a trend, and it is the case for pooling the model's output rather than discarding it. The tail is the problem. Roughly a quarter of panels are outside 5%, and a few are wrong by orders of magnitude — all of them magnetic-susceptibility plots whose axes span decades, where the model settled on the wrong exponent and every value went with it. Nothing in its own output flags which reading that happened to, which is why every curve in the pooled dataset carries a method field and, for model curves, its measured accuracy and trend — so a consumer can filter rather than trust.
